lead: The first update separates bounded agent research from recursive self-improvement and a bubble-state estimate from an imminent-crash prediction. Product monitoring, authorship detection and legislative proposals keep their claims and evidence limits distinct.

The late-morning update separates fictional AI gossip and sampled personas from claims about model intentions. A research-sabotage allegation remains unverified, while European tooling advocacy and Taiwanese stock outflows keep their dates, sources and decision limits explicit.

The afternoon separates actual evaluation-boundary failures from speculation about cryptography and self-improvement. Research proposals, vendor efficiency results and payment trials retain their verification, compute, permission and legal boundaries; unreleased interfaces stay unreleased.

sections.title: Experimental autonomy is not recursive self-improvement
sections.intro: A secondary DeepMind account and a Clay interview describe bounded automation alongside remaining human and infrastructure work.

sections.title: A bubble estimate is not a timed crash forecast
sections.intro: A journalism-derived index emphasizes relative intensity, false alarms and asymmetric decision costs.

sections.title: Agent visibility and authorship detection both raise authority questions
sections.intro: A funded monitoring product and an opinion essay offer different claims about assigning responsibility.

sections.title: Legislative momentum remains distinct from enacted rules
sections.intro: The original policy article was inaccessible, limiting coverage to the attributed feed excerpt.

sections.title: Generated personas are not hidden opinions or stable identities
sections.intro: A fictional group-chat prompt and a sampled animal-persona exercise require different evidence from claims about actual model beliefs.

sections.title: A sabotage allegation is not an experimental result
sections.intro: An opening social post lacks the protocol and artifacts needed to distinguish intent from ordinary research failure.

sections.title: European tooling proposals and Taiwanese outflows have different scopes
sections.intro: One is older policy advocacy; the other is an attributed partial-month financial snapshot.

sections.title: Research assistance is not proof of autonomous discovery
sections.intro: Kimi offers selected credits, while a quantum-gravity preprint and representation-transfer experiments carry distinct scientific limits.

sections.title: Efficiency depends on compute accounting and matched comparisons
sections.intro: LayerStream reports scoped vendor gains; a depth retrospective and scale-dependent-progress analysis keep mechanisms separate from universal forecasts.

sections.title: A primary incident report separates access from broader speculation
sections.intro: OpenAI documents a specific evaluation escape; a thin cryptography headline cannot establish that online security has failed.

sections.title: Agent payments still depend on permission and remedies
sections.intro: A UK pizza trial uses a limited mandate, while Muse liability reporting distinguishes contracts and proposed law.

sections.title: Measurement proposals and dependency discipline address different risks
sections.intro: An RSI essay proposes counterfactuals; engineering commentary asks for inventories and controlled upgrades rather than implicit trust.

sections.title: Roadmaps and hardware workloads are not universal availability
sections.intro: Drive browsing and Hermes designs remain development reports; AMD dashboard measurements have specific workload boundaries.

sections.title: Workplace control and geopolitical effects remain attributed arguments
sections.intro: Doctorow offers a labor analogy, a career post announces a move, and an inaccessible interview story limits export-policy claims.

sections.title: A bouncing-ball interface offers little evidence about prediction quality
sections.intro: The readable game page does not establish its simulation, settlement or any AI mechanism.
